slides.title: Generating Groups
slides.notes: Begin with the chapter question: what algebraic information must be fixed before a group can become geometric? Emphasize that generators give an alphabet, relations say which words collapse, and a Cayley graph turns those choices into a metric object that can later be compared, enlarged, or deformed.

slides.title: From Algebra To Geometry
slides.notes: Use the roadmap as a compression of the chapter. The first lane reviews groups and maps, the middle lanes build presentations from free words and relators, and the final lanes assemble new groups. The lecture keeps asking which algebraic decision becomes visible as an edge, cycle, fiber, or tree.

slides.title: Groups And Homomorphisms
slides.notes: Frame a homomorphism as a structure-preserving lens. The kernel records what becomes invisible, the image records what survives in the target, and the quotient principle explains why normal subgroups matter. This prepares students to see presentations as quotients of free groups rather than as mysterious notation.

slides.title: Generators As An Alphabet
slides.notes: Slow down on the language metaphor. A generating set is not yet geometry by itself, but it lets every element be reached by words. Once a finite generating set is chosen, word length becomes a first distance model, and changing the alphabet changes the local shape of balls.

slides.title: Free Groups Before Relations
slides.notes: The free group slide should feel like the no-identifications baseline. Reduced words cancel adjacent inverse letters and otherwise remain distinct. The rooted tree is useful because every edge appends one generator choice, so cycles are absent until relations are deliberately imposed.

slides.title: The Universal Property
slides.notes: Present the universal property as a routing rule rather than as a slogan. To define a homomorphism from a free group, choose the images of the free generators, then extend by reading words. This is why free groups are the raw material for constructing all generated groups.

slides.title: Relations Create Identifications
slides.notes: Point to the two words before and after the relation is imposed. A relator does not merely add an equation to a list; it forces every conjugate and product consequence to vanish in the quotient. The picture makes the algebraic closure operation feel like glued paths in a graph.

slides.title: Presentations As Machines
slides.notes: Use this slide to connect notation with computation. The presentation first builds the free group on the alphabet, then divides by the normal closure of the chosen relators. In a Cayley graph, short relators become short loops, while missing relators leave branches free to keep expanding.

slides.title: Dihedral Laboratory
slides.notes: The dihedral example is the finite laboratory from the notebook. Rotations stay on one ring, reflections live on the other, and the reflection generator jumps between them. The exact checks make the presentation honest: the displayed loops correspond to identities in the group law, not just attractive symmetry.

slides.title: Cayley Graph Regularity
slides.notes: Stress that regularity is not an accident of drawing style. Every group element has the same available generator moves, so the same degree appears at every vertex when the generating set is fixed. The degree histogram is a compact audit that the graph was built uniformly.

slides.title: Finite Generation Versus Finite Presentation
slides.notes: This is the caution slide. Finite generation gives a finite alphabet, while finite presentation also gives a finite rulebook. The gap matters because a short alphabet can still hide infinitely many necessary relations, and algorithmic questions about whether words collapse can become genuinely hard.

slides.title: Direct Products
slides.notes: Explain direct products as independent motion in two coordinates. A generator from the first factor moves horizontally, and a generator from the second factor moves vertically. The grid preview is not the whole story for every product, but it shows why product constructions often create layered metric geometry.

slides.title: Extensions And Semidirect Products
slides.notes: Use the fiber picture to separate kernel and quotient information. An extension places a normal subgroup over each quotient element, while a semidirect product remembers how the quotient acts on the kernel. The twist arrows warn students that assembling groups is not always a rectangular product.

slides.title: Free Products And Amalgamation
slides.notes: Free products should look like alternating syllables with no forced cancellation between factors. Amalgamation adds a controlled glue: selected subgroups are identified before the alternating word structure expands. This slide previews why Bass-Serre pictures later turn algebraic splittings into trees.

slides.title: HNN Extensions
slides.notes: Treat the stable letter as a corridor generator. It moves from one embedded subgroup to another according to a specified isomorphism, so the group gains a new direction while preserving a prescribed identification. This construction belongs in the deck because it is a standard bridge from presentations to group actions on trees.

slides.title: Notebook Lab
slides.notes: Close by returning to the executable habit. Students should change the rotation order, predict the group order and two-ring shape, then verify the relators and regularity before trusting the picture. The broader lesson is that presentations should produce inspectable geometry plus checks that survive reruns.
